589.title: Life wasted without praise
589.hook: gun gobind gaaio nahee: if you haven't sung His praises, your life is wasted (Salok M9 1, ang 1426)
589.howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's fifty-seven saloks are read near the very end of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, at the bhog ceremony that closes it, often held for weddings, new homes and funerals.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, living his calm, and your line: love without clutching. Did you loosen one grip with someone you love? Today we open the last pages of the Granth, and the ninth Guru's saloks. Day five hundred eighty-nine.
screen: `LIVING HIS CALM — LOVE WITHOUT CLUTCHING.`

segments.voice: At the end of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, after days of continuous recitation, the reader reaches the last few pages. The family who arranged the reading is often sitting close, sometimes after a wedding, sometimes after a death. And what's read near the very end is a run of short couplets by Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Salok Mahalla nine. So these lines are some of the most heard words in Sikh life, at the moments when people are most awake to what matters. The first one is a single breath long, and it doesn't waste a word.
screen: `THE END OF A COMPLETE READING.` → `THE FAMILY SITTING CLOSE.` → `THE FIRST SALOK.`

segments.voice: The first salok begins gun gobind gaaio nahee, janam akaarath keen. In paraphrase: you haven't sung the praises of the Lord of the world; you've made your life useless. Gun means virtues, qualities. Gobind is the Lord who sustains the world. Gaaio is sung. And akaarath is for nothing, to no purpose, close cousin to the akaaj we heard in Jaijavanti. Then the second line, in paraphrase: says Nanak, O mind, love the Lord the way a fish loves water. Stop on that fish. A fish doesn't visit the water now and then. It doesn't praise water once a week. Water is where it breathes. Take it out, and it gasps. That's the kind of praise the salok is talking about. Not a polite compliment, but the thing you can't live without. Notice the verb, too: sung. Sikh devotion is musical from top to bottom. The Granth is set in ragas, kirtan fills the gurdwara, and praise in this tradition is often literally singing. The salok doesn't say a life without praise is evil. It says it's akaarath, unused, like an instrument left in its case. And it's addressed to the mind, man, not to someone else. The Guru isn't scolding a crowd. He's speaking quietly to the inner voice of whoever is listening. There are fifty-seven of these saloks, and over the next days we'll hear them one by one. Short, steady, and very honest about time. The first one sets the tone. While there's time, sing.
screen: `GUN GOBIND GAAIO NAHEE.` · `AKAARATH: A LIFE UNUSED.` · `LIKE A FISH LOVES WATER.` · `PRAISE HERE IS SUNG.` · then, large: `SING, WHILE THERE'S TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing one line of praise. If you know a shabad, or even just Waheguru, sing or hum it softly now, once or several times. Don't worry about your voice. If singing feels strange, try humming one long note and feeling it in your chest. If you don't pray, sing a line of anything that makes you grateful, and let the sound carry the thanks. Then sit quietly and feel what's left in the body after singing. The bell holds the time.
Life wasted without praise. The first salok of Guru Tegh Bahadur says a life that never sings the Lord's virtues goes unused, and asks the mind to love the Lord like a fish loves water.
screen: `LIFE WASTED WITHOUT PRAISE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: sing, while there's time. Today, sing or hum one line out loud, in the car, the shower, the kitchen. Let it be praise. Day five hundred eighty-nine.

screen: `DAY 589 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE DAYS SLIP BY.`

590.title: The days slip by
590.hook: the early saloks warn that days slip away while the mind sleeps (Salok M9, ang 1426)
590.howItsDone: Sikhs hear the ninth Guru's saloks at the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; many know their refrain, kaho naanak, by heart, and take them as reminders that life's time is passing.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-NINETY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, life wasted without praise, and your line: sing, while there's time. Did you sing or hum one line out loud? While there's time, it said. Today the saloks look straight at the time itself. Day five hundred ninety.
screen: `LIFE WASTED WITHOUT PRAISE — SING, WHILE THERE'S TIME.`

segments.voice: Look at a photo from five years ago. The haircut, the phone in your hand, the people beside you. Some of them you still see. Some you haven't spoken to in years. Where did those five years go? You were there for every day of them, and yet most of them have left no trace at all. It's not that you were asleep. You were busy. But busy can be its own kind of sleep. The early saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur keep coming back to this, couplet after couplet, like someone gently shaking a sleeper's shoulder.
screen: `A PHOTO FROM FIVE YEARS AGO.` → `WHERE DID THE DAYS GO?` → `BUSY CAN BE A KIND OF SLEEP.`

segments.voice: The second salok asks, in paraphrase: why are you so absorbed in poisonous things? You don't turn away from them even for an instant. Says Nanak, meditate on the Lord, O mind, and you won't be caught in death's noose. The word for instant is nimakh, the blink of an eye. The salok isn't asking for a whole life of retreat. It asks: could you look up, even for one blink? The third salok ends with a line that sums up this whole run of couplets: your lifespan is passing, slipping away. Auadh is the span of life, the time you were given. And it's going, right now, at exactly the speed of this sentence. Listen to how the saloks repeat themselves, too. Again and again, the second line begins kaho naanak, says Nanak, and then calls the mind: O mind, man re, manaa. They are built like a refrain. That repetition is the teaching. A single warning gets forgotten by lunchtime. A couplet that keeps coming back, day after day, at the end of every reading, wears a groove in you. Notice what the saloks don't say. They don't say the days are bad, or that time spent working or loving is wasted. They say the days slip, and the mind sleeps through them. The cure isn't more hours. It's waking up inside the ones you have, even for the blink of an eye. That's why the practice today is so small. You don't need to change your life to notice it. You just need to look at the clock and really see it.
screen: `WHY SO ABSORBED IN POISON?` · `NIMAKH: ONE BLINK OF AN EYE.` · `AUADH: THE LIFESPAN SLIPPING.` · `KAHO NAANAK: A REFRAIN THAT WAKES.` · then, large: `THE DAYS SLIP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice the time right now. Look at a clock, or your phone's time, and say it to yourself. Then say the date, the day of the week, and where you are. Now close your eyes. This is the only time there is. Feel the breath arrive and leave. Let each breath be a blink of waking, a nimakh. When you drift into plans or replays, come back to the clock's simple fact: it's now. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths. The bell holds the time.
The days slip by. Guru Tegh Bahadur's early saloks warn that our lifespan, auadh, is slipping away, and ask the mind to wake even for a blink.
screen: `THE DAYS SLIP BY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the days slip. Today, three times, look at a clock and actually see it. Say the time, and take one awake breath. Day five hundred ninety.

screen: `DAY 590 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NONE OF IT IS YOURS.`

591.title: None of it is yours
591.hook: wealth, spouse, property: you call them yours, but none goes with you (Salok M9, ang 1426)
591.howItsDone: Sikhs live as householders who work, own and share; the ninth Guru's salok on wealth, spouse and property is often heard at bhog ceremonies after a death, as a reminder that nothing we own goes with us.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-NINETY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the days slip by, and your line: the days slip. Did you look at a clock and really see it? If the days are slipping, what are we holding as they go? Today's salok asks about the word mine. Day five hundred ninety-one.
screen: `THE DAYS SLIP BY — THE DAYS SLIP.`

segments.voice: Clearing out a parent's house after they've died is one of the strangest jobs a person can do. Every drawer is full of things that mattered to someone. The good china saved for guests who rarely came. A box of receipts from 1987. A coat that still smells like them. Each object was mine to someone for decades. Now it's a question: keep, give, throw away. And the one who called it all mine isn't here to decide. Guru Tegh Bahadur's fifth salok stands in exactly that room, and says what everyone in it is thinking.
screen: `CLEARING OUT A PARENT'S HOUSE.` → `EVERY DRAWER WAS SOMEONE'S MINE.` → `THE FIFTH SALOK.`

segments.voice: The salok begins dhan daaraa sampat sagal, jin apunee kar maan. In paraphrase: wealth, spouse, all your property, all the things you take to be your own: not one of them is your companion. Says Nanak, know this as true. Dhan is wealth. Sampat is property, possessions. Daaraa is wife, or spouse. And the key phrase is apunee kar maan: to treat as one's own. That's what the salok is really looking at. Not the things, but the word mine stamped on them. Now, the salok lists a spouse beside the money, and that can sound harsh. But Sikhs are householders. The Gurus married, raised children, ran kitchens and farms. The salok isn't saying don't love your husband or wife. It's saying that even the person closest to you isn't a possession, and doesn't travel with you through death. Hearing it that way, it's almost tender. The people we love were never ours to own. They were gifts, given for a while. And notice the word companion, sangee. The salok isn't asking you to throw anything away. It's asking: who walks with you all the way? On day five hundred twelve, Sukhmani said the earned Name and the self your deeds shaped are what go along. Guru Tegh Bahadur's couplet makes the same point from the other side, by naming what stays behind. The practical result is a lighter grip. You can enjoy a good house, love a family, earn honestly, and still say, quietly: this is lent to me. None of it goes. That's not a loss. It's the truth that frees your hands.
screen: `DHAN, DAARAA, SAMPAT.` · `APUNEE KAR MAAN: CALLING IT MINE.` · `PEOPLE AREN'T POSSESSIONS.` · `WHAT IS LENT, NOT OWNED.` · then, large: `NONE OF IT GOES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one possession lightly. Pick up something you own and care about: a ring, a watch, a mug, your phone. Hold it in an open hand. Feel its weight. Think about where it came from and who made it. Then say quietly to yourself: this is lent to me. Notice what happens in your chest. Does the grip tighten, or loosen? Put it down gently and sit with empty hands for the rest of the time. If you pray, you can give thanks to Waheguru for what's been lent. The bell holds the time.
None of it is yours. The fifth salok says wealth, spouse and property, everything we call our own, is not our companion all the way; know this as true.
screen: `NONE OF IT IS YOURS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: none of it goes. Today, when you catch yourself saying my, my car, my desk, my time, add the word lent, and see how it changes your grip. Day five hundred ninety-one.

screen: `DAY 591 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LORD IN EVERY HEART.`

592.title: The Lord in every heart
592.hook: ghatt ghatt mai har joo basai: the Lord dwells in every heart, as the holy proclaim (Salok M9, ang 1427)
592.howItsDone: Sikhs serve langar to anyone who comes, seated together on the floor, and remember Bhai Ghanaiya, who gave water to the wounded on both sides, as a model of seeing the Lord in every heart.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-NINETY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, none of it is yours, and your line: none of it goes. Did you add the word lent to one thing you called mine? If nothing we own goes along, what is it that's truly near? Today's salok answers. Day five hundred ninety-two.
screen: `NONE OF IT IS YOURS — NONE OF IT GOES.`

segments.voice: Sikh tradition tells of a man named Bhai Ghanaiya. During the battles around Anandpur, he carried a water skin across the battlefield and gave water to the wounded, to Sikhs and to the soldiers they were fighting. Some Sikhs were furious and brought him before Guru Gobind Singh. The Guru asked him why he was helping the enemy. And Bhai Ghanaiya is remembered as answering that he saw no enemy. In every face, he said, he saw only the Guru. The Guru, the story says, gave him ointment as well, and told him to bandage their wounds too.
screen: `BHAI GHANAIYA'S WATER SKIN.` → `WATER FOR BOTH SIDES.` → `IN EVERY FACE, THE GURU.`

segments.voice: Bhai Ghanaiya's answer is almost a quotation of today's salok, written by Guru Gobind Singh's own father. Ghatt ghatt mai har joo basai, santan kahio pukaar. In paraphrase: the Lord dwells in every heart; the holy ones have proclaimed it aloud. Then: says Nanak, meditate on Him, O mind, and you'll cross the terrifying ocean. Ghatt is a lovely word. It means a clay pot, a vessel, and from that, the body or heart that holds a life. Ghatt ghatt: pot after pot, every single vessel. Not just the devout ones, or the kind ones, or our own people. Every vessel. And pukaar means a loud call, a shout. The holy haven't whispered this truth. They've called it out across the centuries. Last week, in the forest hymn, the Lord was within like scent in a flower: that was about finding God inside yourself. This salok turns the same truth outward. If the Lord lives in my heart, He lives in yours. And in the stranger's. And in the soldier on the other side. That's what makes it hard. It's easy to believe God is in the people we love. The salok doesn't let us stop there. It's the reason Sikh langar feeds anyone who walks in, of any faith or none, seated together on the floor. It's why seva, service, isn't reserved for members. In every heart means every heart. And Bhai Ghanaiya's water skin is what that line looks like when someone actually believes it.
screen: `GHATT GHATT: EVERY VESSEL.` · `PUKAAR: THE HOLY CALL IT ALOUD.` · `TURNED OUTWARD: THE STRANGER TOO.` · `LANGAR FEEDS ANYONE.` · then, large: `IN EVERY HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see Him in one heart. Bring to mind one person you find difficult. Not your worst enemy, just someone who annoys you, or someone you've written off. Picture their face. Now picture the salok's clay vessel, and inside it, the same light that's in you. You don't have to like them. Just let the thought sit: the Lord dwells here too. Notice what softens, and what resists. If you pray, you can hold them before Waheguru for one breath. The bell holds the time.
The Lord in every heart. Ghatt ghatt mai har joo basai: the twelfth salok says the Lord lives in every vessel, every heart, as the holy proclaim aloud.
screen: `THE LORD IN EVERY HEART — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: in every heart. Today, do one small kindness for someone you'd normally pass by, or someone on the other side of an argument. Day five hundred ninety-two.

593.title: Untouched by pain and pleasure
593.hook: the one untouched by pleasure, pain, greed, attachment and pride is the Lord's image (Salok M9, ang 1427)
593.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok among the ninth Guru's saloks at the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and often cite it to say that a person free of craving and pride shows the image of God.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-NINETY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lord in every heart, and your line: in every heart. Did you do one kindness for someone you'd usually pass by? The Lord lives in every vessel. Today's salok says what it looks like when that light shines through. Day five hundred ninety-three.
screen: `THE LORD IN EVERY HEART — IN EVERY HEART.`

segments.voice: Watch someone near the bakery counter at the end of a long day. The smell hits. The craving arrives like a wave: just one, you deserve it, you've had a terrible afternoon. They stand there. And sometimes, if they simply wait, something surprising happens. The wave crests, and then it falls. Thirty seconds later, the want is smaller. Two minutes later, it's gone. Cravings feel permanent from the inside. They almost never are. The thirteenth salok of Guru Tegh Bahadur describes a person these waves can't knock over, and then gives that person a startling name.
screen: `THE BAKERY COUNTER.` → `A CRAVING, LIKE A WAVE.` → `IT CRESTS, THEN FALLS.`

segments.voice: The salok says, in paraphrase: the one whom pleasure and pain don't touch, nor greed, attachment or pride: says Nanak, listen, O mind, that one is the very image of God. The key verb is parsai, to touch, to brush against. These waves come to everyone. The salok doesn't say this person never meets pleasure or pain, greed or pride. It says they come and don't stick, like rain running down a window while the glass stays clear. Then the startling name: moorat bhagvaan, the image of God. Moorat means a form, an image, the word used for statues in temples. Sikhs don't worship images. And yet here, in the last pages of the Granth, the ninth Guru uses that very word for a living person. Not a statue, but someone free. If you want to see what God looks like, the salok says, look at a human being whose heart isn't pushed around. You might remember the Mool Mantar, the opening of the Granth, which calls God akaal moorat, the form beyond time. The same word, moorat. In the Mool Mantar it describes the Timeless. In this salok it describes a person who has become clear enough to show it. Notice how this builds on yesterday. The Lord lives in every heart. Most of the time the waves of craving and pride cover the light, the way waves cover the sand. When they settle, it shows. So becoming untouched isn't about becoming hard. It's about becoming clear, so the One already inside can be seen.
screen: `PARSAI: THE WAVES DON'T STICK.` · `MOORAT BHAGVAAN: GOD'S IMAGE.` · `AKAAL MOORAT, THE SAME WORD.` · `CLEAR ENOUGH TO SHOW THE LIGHT.` · then, large: `UNTOUCHED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one craving pass. Sit and breathe, and wait for any want to arise: to check your phone, to snack, to move, to stop sitting. When it comes, don't act and don't fight. Just watch it, like a wave. Feel where it sits in the body. Notice it rise, crest, and begin to fall. Count the breaths it takes. If another comes, watch that one too. You're practicing being touched without being moved. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths. The bell holds the time.
Untouched by pain and pleasure. The thirteenth salok calls the one whom pleasure, pain, greed, attachment and pride don't touch moorat bhagvaan, the very image of God.
screen: `UNTOUCHED BY PAIN AND PLEASURE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: untouched. Today, when a craving comes, wait three breaths before you act. Just three. Watch the wave, and see what's left. Day five hundred ninety-three.

594.title: Gold and iron alike
594.hook: the one to whom praise and blame, gold and iron are the same (Salok M9, ang 1427)
594.howItsDone: Sikhs hear the fourteenth salok among Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks at the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and speak of jeevan mukat, being free while alive, as its ideal.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-NINETY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, untouched by pain and pleasure, and your line: untouched. Did you wait three breaths when a craving came? Yesterday's salok was about the waves inside us. Today's is about the voices outside. Day five hundred ninety-four.
screen: `UNTOUCHED BY PAIN AND PLEASURE — UNTOUCHED.`

segments.voice: A performance review lands in your inbox. There are four paragraphs of praise, and one line that says you could communicate more clearly. Guess which line you'll be thinking about at two in the morning. Most of us are built this way. We can hear ninety-nine compliments and carry one criticism home like a stone in a shoe. Or the reverse: one big compliment and we float for days, and then we need another. Either way, someone else's voice is holding the steering wheel. Guru Tegh Bahadur's fourteenth salok describes a person who has taken the wheel back.
screen: `FOUR PARAGRAPHS OF PRAISE.` → `ONE LINE AT 2AM.` → `WHO HOLDS THE WHEEL?`

segments.voice: The salok begins ustat nindiaa naahi jih, kanchan loh samaan. In paraphrase: the one for whom there is no praise and no slander, to whom gold and iron are the same: says Nanak, listen, O mind, know that one to be liberated. Ustat is praise. Nindiaa is slander, blame, talking someone down. Kanchan is gold, and loh is iron, the everyday metal of pots and plows. And samaan is equal, alike. The salok doesn't say this person never gets praised or blamed. It says praise and blame have no place in them, no hook to catch on. And then it sets two metals side by side. Gold glitters, it's what we'd like to be called. Iron is ordinary. Imagine being as calm when someone calls you iron as when someone calls you gold. Back in the Sorath hymn, twelve days ago, we met gold and dust seen alike. Here it's gold and iron. The ninth Guru keeps returning to this picture, as if to say it's worth hearing more than once. And notice the last word: mukat, liberated. Sikh teaching speaks of jeevan mukat, someone free while still alive. Freedom here isn't a place you go after death. It's a person at a desk, reading a review, who can take the four paragraphs of praise and the one line of criticism with the same steady face, learn from both, and stay themselves. That's the practice: not to stop hearing what people say, but to stop being steered by it.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one compliment and one criticism calmly. Sit and breathe. Bring back the last compliment you got. Feel the little lift it gives, and let it settle. Now bring back a recent criticism. Feel the sting, and let that settle too. Hold them side by side, like a gold coin and an iron nail in your two open hands. Ask of each: is there something true here I can learn? Then set both down. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths. The bell holds the time.
Gold and iron alike. The fourteenth salok says the one for whom praise and blame, gold and iron, are the same is mukat, free.
screen: `GOLD AND IRON ALIKE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: gold and iron alike. Today, when someone praises or criticizes you, say thank you in the same tone for both, then ask what's true in it. Day five hundred ninety-four.

595.title: Fear none, frighten none
595.hook: bhai kaahoo kau det neh neh bhai maanat aan: frighten no one and fear no one; that one is wise (Salok M9, ang 1427)
595.tomorrow: Like a dream and a show
595.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom each year, especially at Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Delhi, and often recite his salok on giving and taking no fear as the heart of his example.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-NINETY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, gold and iron alike, and your line: gold and iron alike. Did you meet praise and criticism in the same tone? This week the saloks said: sing while there's time, the days slip, none of it goes, the Lord is in every heart, untouched. Today, a salok many Sikhs link to his life. Day five hundred ninety-five.
screen: `GOLD AND IRON ALIKE.`

segments.voice: Think of the two kinds of people who make a room go tense. One is the bully: loud, threatening, used to getting their way by making others afraid. The other is the person so afraid themselves that they'll agree to anything, betray anyone, to stay safe. They look like opposites. But they're often the same person on different days. Fear going out, and fear coming in, are two ends of one rope. Guru Tegh Bahadur's sixteenth salok cuts that rope at both ends, in a single line.
screen: `THE BULLY AND THE FRIGHTENED.` → `TWO ENDS OF ONE ROPE.` → `ONE LINE CUTS BOTH.`

segments.voice: The salok says bhai kaahoo kau det neh, neh bhai maanat aan. In paraphrase: the one who gives fear to no one, and accepts fear from no one else: says Nanak, listen, O mind, call that one wise. Bhai is fear. Det is to give. Maanat is to accept, to take on. So: not handing fear out, and not taking it in. The wise one, giaanee, is defined by both at once. Sikhs hear this line beside two words from the Mool Mantar, the opening of the Granth: nirbhau, without fear, and nirvair, without enmity. Those describe God. This salok describes a person who has started to resemble them. And then Sikhs think of the man who wrote it. Sikh tradition remembers that in 1675, a group of Kashmiri Pandits, Hindus, came to him at Anandpur. They said Mughal officials were forcing them to give up their faith. He listened, and set out for Delhi himself. He raised no army. He threatened no one. On the way he was arrested and taken to Delhi. And when he was ordered to give up his own faith or die, he refused. He was executed in Delhi, at the place where Gurdwara Sis Ganj stands today. Sikhs call him Hind di Chadar, the shield of India, and remember that he gave his life for the freedom of people whose faith was not his own. Frighten none, fear none. He didn't frighten his enemies, and he didn't let them frighten him. That's a very hard kind of courage, gentle and brave in the same moment, and the salok makes it sound almost simple.
screen: `BHAI: NOT GIVEN, NOT TAKEN.` · `NIRBHAU, NIRVAIR.` · `ANANDPUR TO DELHI, 1675.` · `HIND DI CHADAR.` · then, large: `FRIGHTEN NONE, FEAR NONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be gentle and brave once. Sit and breathe. Think of one situation coming up where fear might show up on either end: where you might lean on someone too hard, or give in when you shouldn't. A meeting, a family conversation, a moment of standing up for someone. Picture yourself in it, speaking calmly and clearly, neither pushing nor shrinking. Feel your feet on the floor. If you pray, you can ask Waheguru for that steadiness. The bell holds the time.
Fear none. The sixteenth salok calls wise the one who frightens no one and accepts fear from no one, and Sikhs see it lived in Guru Tegh Bahadur's walk to Delhi.
screen: `FEAR NONE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: frighten none, fear none. Today, in one tense moment, lower your voice instead of raising it, and don't back down from what's right. Day five hundred ninety-five.

screen: `DAY 595 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: LIKE A DREAM AND A SHOW.`
